Unpublished Report Warns Feral Deer Threaten Australia Unless Urgent Action Is Taken

30 Oct 2026, 10:26 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Climate Desk · Source: www.theguardian.com

An unpublished government assessment has warned that Australia is largely failing to contain the spread of feral deer, with experts cautioning that the invasive species risks becoming the country’s next major agricultural and environmental crisis alongside feral pigs.

The findings, drawn from an evaluation of the national feral deer action plan covering the period from 2020 to 2025, highlight that deer have both increased in total numbers and expanded their territorial range. According to the report, the pests currently cost more than $91 million annually in production losses and management expenditures across Australia.

Jurisdictional Findings and Expert Concerns

The national vertebrate pest management report card, compiled by the National Vertebrate Pest Coordinators, evaluated states and territories using a traffic-light grading system across four distinct categories. The findings indicate widespread struggles in controlling the animals:

  • South Australia: Received a green rating in all four assessed categories, demonstrating successful decreases in deer abundance, distribution, and overall environmental and agricultural impacts following an ambitious statewide eradication plan launched in 2022.
  • New South Wales and Tasmania: Received red ratings across all four categories.
  • Queensland and the Australian Capital Territory: Received three red ratings and one yellow rating.

Professor Euan Ritchie of Deakin University, president of the Australian Mammal Society, stated that the report reflects a sustained failure by governments to invest adequately in population control. He noted that deer populations create severe consequences for agriculture, native ecosystems, road safety, and culturally significant sites.

Six feral deer species are currently established in Australia: chital, fallow, hog, red, rusa, and sambar. The highest population densities are concentrated in south-eastern Australia, alongside smaller, localized populations in South Australia, Western Australia, and the Northern Territory.

Economic Arguments and the Path Forward

Advocacy groups and researchers emphasize that targeted interventions could still alter the trajectory of the spread. Reece Pianta, advocacy manager for the Invasive Species Council, described deer as Australia's next potential feral pig, noting that early intervention could still contain or reverse population growth.

In South Australia, where an agricultural impact estimate previously projected that annual damage costs could climb from $36 million to $241 million by 2031, a $4 million eradication program has yielded measurable declines. Professor Andrew Lowe of the Adelaide University Environment Institute noted that achieving functional eradication in the state would require an estimated additional investment of $10 million over the next decade, contrasted against the massive potential costs of inaction.

Practical Implications and Verification

Readers seeking to understand the broader context of invasive species management in Australia can review official updates and environmental assessments through the Guardian Australia environment section or official government agricultural department publications.

  • Confirmed Facts: The unpublished report evaluates the 2020–2025 national feral deer action plan; feral deer currently cost over $91 million annually in management and production losses; South Australia is the only jurisdiction that received positive marks across all evaluated categories.
  • Unknowns: The full, unabridged text of the government report remains unpublished outside of leaked findings reviewed by advocacy groups, and long-term funding commitments across other states remain unconfirmed.
  • How to Verify: Readers can consult original reporting and official environmental policy trackers via [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/30/australia-feral-deer-problem-report-national-action-plan).
